We, thus, preregistered to only discuss events for which we could detect at least medium-sized effects (n ≥ 73) in the main manuscript. Other events were still analyzed but are only reported in the Supplementary Materials (https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915).

Results

This manuscript is accompanied by an HTML file containing the analysis code, all results, and supplementary analyses. As described above, we deviated in two ways from the preregistration (i.e., focus on robust event occurrences and inclusion of testing effects). Results of models as preregistered can be found in Section 6 of the Supplementary Materials (https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915).

Descriptive Statistics

Table 2 summarizes the number of event occurrences in the sample. New romantic relationship (n = 794), first sexual intercourse (n = 767), finished education (n = 637), and relationship breakup (n = 628) were the most frequently experienced events. Importantly, for all life events except marriage and bought a house, the sample sizes were sufficient to identify at least medium-sized effects. Further descriptive statistics can be found in Section 1 of the Supplementary Materials (https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915). Note. These samples sizes of the event groups refer to "robust event occurrences", meaning that participants had to report a respective life change at two consecutive assessments. This way of capturing life events was a deviation from the preregistration to deal with inconsistencies in participants' reporting.

Event-Related Changes in Agency

Event-related changes in agency are illustrated in Figure 1. As can be seen in this figure, several life events were associated with significant within-person decreases in agency. First sexual intercourse predicted decreases in agency in the year before (d = -0.24, p = .003), the year after (d = -0.32, p < .001), and 2 years after the event (d = -0.30, p = .003), with linear contrasts among event-related dummies indicating that agency significantly decreased from assessments 2 years prior the first sexual intercourse to assessments up to 2 years thereafter.

Furthermore, we found significant within-person decreases in agency in the year before childbirth (d = -0.32, p = .005), 2 years before a relationship breakup (d = -0.22, p = .002), 1 year before getting a driver's license (d = -0.48, p = .003), and 1 year after graduation (d = -0.20, p = .008). Finally, moving away from the caregiver was associated with event-related changes in agency in the year before (d = -0.27, p = .002) and the year after (d = -0.27, p = .001) the event occurrence, with linear contrasts pointing to a significant decrease in agency from 2 years before moving away from caregiver to assessments 1 year thereafter.

Most of these effects were replicated in the simplified model that only considered prevs. post-event changes. Specifically, we found significant decreases in agency after the first sexual intercourse (d = -0.32, p < .001) and after moving away from the caregiver (d = -0.24, p = .003), as well as decreases before childbirth (d = -0.29, p = .005) and a relationship breakup (d = -0.21, p = .001). Overall, our findings were in line with Hypothesis 2 that childbirth predicts decreases in agency, while Hypothesis 1 (marriage predicts decreases in agency) could not be formally tested due to the low sample size for this event. Event-Related Changes in Agency Note. This figure illustrates event-related changes in agency in the years surrounding the occurrence of different life events. Significant within-person changes (p < .01) in the years prior to or after a certain life event-compared to assessments unrelated to the event occurrence-are depicted in black. Error bars indicate 99% confidence intervals.

Event-Related Changes in Communion

Event-related changes in communion are illustrated in Figure 2. Similar to the effects for agency, several life events predicted within-person decreases in communion. First, communion decreased in the year before a relationship breakup (d = -0.22, p = .004). Second, finishing education predicted decreases in communion in the year before (d = -0.28, p < .001) and the year after (d = -0.23, p = .003) the event occurrence. Finally, there were significant within-person decreases in communion 1 year before (d = -0.51, p < .001), 1 year after (d = -0.48, p = .001), 2 years after (d = -0.42, p = .004), and more than 2 years (d = -0.56, p = .001) after obtaining a driver's license.

All of these effects were replicated in the simplified model (-0.44 ≤ d ≤ -0.20). In addition, we found significant decreases in communion after the first sexual intercourse in that model (d = -0.24, p = .007). In sum, findings were not in line with Hypothesis 4 (start full-time employed predicts increases in communion) and contrary to Hypothesis 3 (finishing education predicts increases in communion). Event-Related Changes in Communion Note. This figure illustrates event-related changes in communion in the years surrounding the occurrence of different life events. Significant within-person changes (p < .01) in the years prior to or after a certain life eventcompared to assessments unrelated to the event occurrence-are depicted in black. Error bars indicate 99% confidence intervals.

Event-Related Changes in Life Satisfaction

Event-related changes in life satisfaction are illustrated in Figure 3. Life satisfaction significantly increased 2 years before (d = 0.25, p < .001), 1 year before (d = 0.34, p < .001), 1 year after (d = 0.39, p < .001), 2 years after (d = 0.49, p < .001), and more than 2 years after (d = 0.50, p < .001) obtaining a driver's license. In addition, linear contrasts among eventrelated dummies indicated changes in life satisfaction from specific pre-event to specific postevent assessments. For example, life satisfaction significantly increased from assessments 1 to 2 years prior to a new romantic relationship to assessments more than 2 years thereafter, whereas life satisfaction significantly decreased from assessments 1 to 2 years prior to job loss to assessments 1 year thereafter. Similarly, life satisfaction significantly increased from the year before starting full-time employment to assessments 1 to 2 years thereafter.

While similar effects emerged for linear contrasts between pre-and post-event dummies in the simplified model, the within-person increases in life satisfaction surrounding obtaining a driver's license were not replicated. Overall, findings were partially in line with Hypothesis 5 (new romantic relationship predicts increases in life satisfaction), Hypothesis 10 (starting fulltime employed predicts increases in life satisfaction), and Hypothesis 11 (job loss predicts decreases in life satisfaction), whereas we found no supporting evidence for Hypothesis 7 (childbirth predicts increases in life satisfaction), Hypothesis 8 (relationship breakup predicts decreases in life satisfaction), and Hypothesis 9 (finishing education predicts increases in life satisfaction).

Hypothesis 6 (marriage predicts increases in life satisfaction) could not be formally tested due to the low sample size for this event. Event-Related Changes in Life Satisfaction Note. This figure illustrates event-related changes in life satisfaction in the years surrounding the occurrence of different life events. Significant within-person changes (p < .01) in the years prior to or after a certain life eventcompared to assessments unrelated to the event occurrence-are depicted in black. Error bars indicate 99% confidence intervals.

Event-Related Changes in Mental Health

Event-related changes in mental health are illustrated in Figure 4. The only event significantly related to within-person changes in mental health was first sexual intercourse.

Specifically, mental health significantly decreased 2 years before (d = -0.23, p = .007), 1 year before (d = -0.31, p = .001), 1 year after (d = -0.42, p < .001), 2 years after (d = -0.38, p < .001), and more than 2 years after (d = -0.37, p = .001) first sexual intercourse. This effect was replicated in the simplified model, indicating significant decreases in mental health before (d = -0.28, p < .001) and after (d = -0.41, p < .001) having first sexual intercourse. These findings were thus not in line with any of the preregistered hypotheses.

Exploratory Analyses: Mental Health Subscales

In exploratory analyses, we examined event-related changes in specific mental health problems. These analyses showed that the decreases in mental health in the years surrounding first sexual intercourse were primarily driven by increases in depression, anxiety, life stress, and interpersonal conflicts but not-for example-sleep issues and anger issues. In addition, we found increases in substance abuse in the years surrounding graduation and increases in anxiety in the years surrounding obtaining a driver's license (see Section 4 of the https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915 for details).

Exploratory Analyses: Gender and Country Differences

In an additional exploratory analysis step, we examined whether event-related changes differed between men and women and among the three countries included in ALLS. Results of this analysis can be found in Section 5 of the https://osf.io/ed293/files/z96mc?view_only=c126a6715ba647f2abde62bb50f59915. Overall, we found limited evidence for gender differences in event-related changes. The only exception was that women decreased more in their communion after their first sexual intercourse than men.

Furthermore, we found several differences in event-related changes across the three countries. For example, emerging adults living in Kenya showed stronger agency decreases after experiencing a relationship breakup or finishing education than emerging adults in South Africa. Similarly, emerging adults living in Kenya showed stronger decreases in their communion after a new relationship or childbirth than emerging adults in Namibia. Discussion

The present study is one of the first examinations of event-related changes in sub-Saharan Africa. Using data from young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, we found that agency and/or communion decreased among individuals who became a parent, finished education, or obtained a driver's license. Furthermore, life satisfaction increased for participants getting their driver's license, and mental health decreased in the years surrounding their first sexual intercourse. In the following, we discuss different possible interpretations of our results and reasons why event-related changes may have diverged from those reported in Western contexts.

The key take-away of this study is that event-related changes in personality traits, mental health, and life satisfaction seem to differ across cultural contexts as only one of our generalizability hypotheses was supported. The only finding that converged with prior metaanalyses from Western contexts was that childbirth predicted decreases in agency (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026). Becoming a parent and caring for an infant is associated with new responsibilities and challenges, which may undermine feelings of competence and confidence, and decrease opportunities to show agentic behaviors such as asserting oneself at work or going out with friends.

Other events substantially diverged in their effects from Western findings. For example, finishing education predicted decreases rather than increases in agency and communion. There may be methodological or substantive reasons for these differences. Methodologically, emerging adults in sub-Saharan Africa may be less experienced with filling out questionnaires than over-researched student samples from Western countries. This could lead to differences in response biases, socially desirable responding, and willingness to disclose personal experiences (e.g., Tellis & Chandrasekaran, 2010), all of which may influence results on event-related changes in personality and well-being. Furthermore, linguistic misunderstandings may have resulted in inconsistent reporting of life events, potentially blurring results on event-related changes, which is why we decided to focus on events that were consistently reported in our main analyses.

Substantively, there may be differences in the meaning of life events across cultural contexts. For example, while finishing education is often viewed as a positive milestone associated with employment, financial independence, and adult role attainment in Western countries, these outcomes may not always be readily accessible to emerging adults in contexts characterized by high unemployment and economic uncertainty (Levy & Dubinsky, 2024). For young adults living in sub-Saharan Africa, finishing education may signal entry into a period of uncertainty during which anticipated opportunities fail to materialize, potentially undermining agency and communion. Supporting this interpretation, decreases in agency after finishing education were highest for young adults living in Kenya, the ALLS country with the highest youth unemployment rate (Federation of Kenya Employers, 2024).

Similarly, first sexual intercourse seems to differ in its mental health implications across cultural contexts. In Western countries, first sexual intercourse tends to be either unrelated to well-being or associated with transient increases in life satisfaction and self-esteem-consistent with the fulfillment of a developmental milestone (Andrae et al., 2025). In contrast, mental health significantly decreased in the years surrounding first sexual intercourse in young adults living in sub-Saharan Africa. There is initial evidence from South Africa indicating that the circumstances surrounding the sexual debut which can include coercion, sexual violence, and health risks are important in understanding this association (McClinton Appollis et al., 2022; Seff et al., 2021). First sexual intercourse may be associated with poorer mental health where it occurs within contexts of coercion and adverse health consequences.

Overall, our pattern of results points to broader cross-cultural differences in the developmental significance of emerging adulthood. While emerging adulthood is typically seen as a phase of exploration and growth in Western countries (Arnett, 2007), structural barriers and constraints may complicate these developmental trajectories in sub-Saharan Africa. This interpretation is also consistent with the concept of Waithood (Honwana, 2019), which describes emerging adulthood in sub-Saharan Africa as a a prolonged and often involuntary period between socially recognized adulthood and dependence due to structural and economic constraints.

However, it is also noteworthy that some event-related changes-especially those in life satisfaction and mental health-did not follow the typical adaptation pattern, with the most pronounced effects in the first year after the event occurrence, then slowly attenuating (Haehner, Krämer, et al., 2026; Krämer et al., 2025). This raises questions about whether these events were responsible for the observed changes, or whether they are proxies for other changes. We aimed to come close to the causal relevance of life events by accounting for stable betweenperson differences with fixed-effects regressions and controlling for within-person age and testing effects. However, other experiences that co-occur with the examined life events could still confound the observed effects. For example, improvements in the financial situation may predict both getting a driver's license-as driving lessons are relatively costly-and increases in life satisfaction, which could explain why we found increases in life satisfaction when participants obtained their driver's license. Future research should therefore investigate how emerging adults in sub-Saharan Africa experience important life events and how these events are associated with changes in their everyday lives.

Limitations

The present study has several limitations. First, although the overall sample size of ALLS is relatively large, the sample size for specific events was sometimes limited. For example, we could not test our hypotheses for getting married as this event was too rare in the examined age group. Second, by relying on demographic status changes and a fixed set of directly measured life events, we may have missed other contextually important life changes (Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2026). Third, we exclusively relied on self-reports to examine event-related changes, which are prone to biases such as socially desirable responding or acquiescence.

Conclusion

Life events have been theorized to be important drivers of changes in personality traits and well-being. However, prior evidence on these effects stemmed almost exclusively from Western countries. Using a large longitudinal sample of young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, we examined the cross-cultural generalizability of event-related changes in personality traits, life satisfaction, and mental health. Although we found several significant event-related changes, findings diverged substantially from Western results. Future crosscultural research is needed to test the replicability of our findings and to investigate different explanations for why findings may differ across cultural contexts.
